=={{header|Cxc}}==

Cxc has no recursive functions; recursion folds into the atom lifecycle. The two running fields <code>a</code> and <code>b</code> hold <code>(F(i), F(i+1))</code>, the state-space representation of the order-2 recurrence. Each <code>tick</code> prints <code>a</code>, advances <code>(a, b)</code> to <code>(b, a + b)</code> via the <code>=></code> transition arrow (one-shot field update for the next state), increments <code>i</code>, and self-sends. The terminal arm with guard <code>i >= 20</code> fires first under source-order dispatch, so the self-loop arm runs only while <code>i</code> is below the fence.

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
def main:
    a: Int! = 0
    b: Int! = 1
    i: Int! = 0

    -> running
        then: self :> tick

    running <: tick -> end
        |: i >= 20

    running <: tick -> running
        then:
            print(a)
            a => b
            b => a + b
            i => i + 1
            self :> tick
</syntaxhighlight>

The <code>=></code> arrow is distinct from assignment: it declares the new value of a field for the next state. Within a single arm body, reads of <code>a</code>/<code>b</code> see the entry snapshot, so <code>b => a + b</code> uses the pre-tick <code>a</code> even though the preceding line stages a new <code>a</code>. Two scalars are load-bearing because Fibonacci is a 2nd-order recurrence; one scalar won't carry the state.
